name: Raymond Petrov
presenting_complaint: Sudden severe abdominal and back pain with collapse

medical_history.social: 60 pack-year smoking history, quit 2 years ago. Lives with wife. Retired mechanic. Independent ADLs.
medical_history.family: Brother had an abdominal aortic aneurysm repair aged 70.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: Raymond Petrov, a 74-year-old male ex-smoker, is brought in by ambulance with sudden severe central abdominal pain radiating to the back, and a brief collapse at home. He is pale, clammy and diaphoretic. BP 82/48, HR 124, GCS 14. Ambulance noted a pulsatile, tender central abdominal mass. He is agitated and mottled at the knees.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Sudden-onset severe central abdominal pain radiating through to the back, with syncope/collapse
SOCRATES of pain: tearing/constant, sudden peak, radiation to back/flank/groin
Cardiovascular risk factors: heavy smoking history, hypertension, PVD, age, male sex
Family history of abdominal aortic aneurysm (brother)
Screen for known AAA / prior aortic imaging or surveillance; anticoagulant/antiplatelet use (on aspirin)
Key negatives: no chest pain radiation typical of ACS, no melaena/haematemesis, time of onset and pre-syncope
objective: Immediate A-E assessment; recognise haemorrhagic/hypovolaemic shock (hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, mottling)
Palpate for pulsatile expansile central abdominal mass and abdominal/flank tenderness
Assess peripheral pulses (femoral, popliteal, pedal) and limb perfusion for distal ischaemia
Bedside FAST/aortic ultrasound at the bedside if credentialed (do NOT transfer to CT if unstable)
ECG to exclude ACS mimic and continuous cardiac monitoring; large-bore IV access
VBG for lactate/Hb, and serial BP with the patient kept talking (mentation as perfusion marker)
assessment: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm until proven otherwise (pulsatile mass + hypotension + back pain)
Haemorrhagic shock secondary to contained/free aortic rupture
Differential to consider: aortic dissection, renal/ureteric colic, perforated viscus, myocardial infarction, mesenteric ischaemia
plan: Call vascular surgery and the ED consultant NOW; activate theatre, ICU and (if regional) retrieval simultaneously
Two large-bore (14-16G) IV cannulae; send urgent crossmatch and activate the massive transfusion protocol
Permissive hypotension: aim systolic ~80-90 mmHg (a systolic that keeps him talking); do NOT over-resuscitate with crystalloid
IV opioid analgesia titrated (e.g. fentanyl 25-50 microg IV increments) with close monitoring
Urgent bloods: FBC, UEC, coagulation profile, group and crossmatch (6 units), VBG/lactate
Definitive management is emergency theatre (open repair or EVAR) - transfer the resuscitating patient directly to theatre, not to the scanner
Bedside aortic ultrasound only if it does not delay theatre; keep patient nil by mouth, catheterise, warm the patient

critical_errors: Sending the haemodynamically unstable patient to CT instead of straight to theatre - an unstable patient goes to theatre, not to the scanner
Aggressive fluid/blood over-resuscitation to a normal blood pressure instead of permissive hypotension (worsens rupture bleeding)
Failing to call vascular surgery and activate theatre immediately (treating this as an undifferentiated abdominal pain work-up)
must_not_miss: Ruptured AAA diagnosed clinically and acted on without waiting for imaging
Massive transfusion protocol activated with crossmatched blood
Aortic dissection considered in the differential
Immediate senior/vascular surgical involvement and theatre activation
